answer: True positive: the searchCustomers handler builds a native SQL string with the caller-supplied q interpolated inside quotes and passes it to cds.run, so a quote in q changes the query; the function is reachable by any authenticated user. The rule should be accepted; fix by binding the value, e.g. SELECT.from(Customers).columns('ID','name').where({ name: { like: `%${q}%` } }).

findings.title: SQL injection in searchCustomers (true positive)
findings.statement: req.data.q is the unbound String parameter of the unbound function searchCustomers and is placed verbatim into a SQL string literal that cds.run executes as native SQL; nothing escapes or validates q before. A value containing a single quote breaks out of the LIKE literal, allowing reads of other columns/tables (e.g. Customers email and phone, which the service projection hides).

evidence.quote: return cds.run(`SELECT ID, name FROM sales_Customers WHERE name LIKE '%${req.data.q}%'`)
function searchCustomers(q : String) returns array of { ID : UUID; name : String };

findings.test: GET /orders/searchCustomers(q='zz'' OR 1=1 --') as alice: a 200 returning all customers (instead of none) confirms the injection.

findings.title: Only authentication guards the function
findings.statement: searchCustomers has no @restrict of its own; the only check is the service-level @requires 'authenticated-user', so every logged-in user (Buyer, Approver, or a user without roles) can send the injectable request.
